questions.question: What is the main purpose of a domain separation tag (DST) in hash-to-curve constructions?
options: To make the output point smaller to transmit
To ensure different protocols/purposes do not accidentally hash to the same curve points
To speed up scalar multiplication by caching
To avoid modular reduction when hashing to the field
questions.explanation: DST binds the hash-to-curve output to a specific context so different protocols (or different purposes within a protocol) do not collide on the same points.

questions.question: In RFC 9380, what is the key difference between encode_to_curve (NU suites) and hash_to_curve (RO suites)?
options: NU suites use XOFs while RO suites use hashes
NU suites output points not on the curve, RO suites output points on the curve
NU suites map one field element to the curve, RO suites map two field elements and add the results
NU suites require cofactor clearing, RO suites never do
questions.explanation: RO suites derive two field elements u[0], u[1], map both, add, and then clear the cofactor; NU suites use one u[0] and map once (still with cofactor clearing step).

questions.question: Which pipeline best matches RFC 9380 for a hash_to_curve (RO) suite?
options: P = lift_x(H(msg) mod p)
u = expand_message(msg); P = map_to_curve(u)
u0,u1 = hash_to_field(msg, DST); Q0 = map_to_curve(u0); Q1 = map_to_curve(u1); P = clear_cofactor(Q0 + Q1)
P = random_point(); P = clear_cofactor(P)
questions.explanation: RO suites use hash_to_field to get two field elements, map both, add, and then clear the cofactor to land in the prime-order subgroup.

questions.question: Why does a typical RO suite derive two field elements (u[0], u[1]) instead of one?
options: To make the output point compress better
To get a distribution closer to a random oracle on the target group
To avoid needing square roots in the mapping
To avoid any dependency on the DST
questions.explanation: Using two independent field elements and adding mapped points is part of the construction that achieves random-oracle-like behavior for hash_to_curve.

questions.question: Why is cofactor clearing included in the RFC 9380 pipeline, even if P-256 has cofactor 1?
options: Because cofactor clearing changes the curve equation
Because RO suites require cofactor clearing but NU suites do not
Because many curves have cofactor > 1 and require subgroup projection; keeping the step prevents omissions when switching curves
Because it hides the DST from attackers
questions.explanation: On curves with cofactor > 1, cofactor clearing is essential to land in the prime-order subgroup. For P-256 it is the identity, but the step is still part of the standard pipeline.

questions.question: Attack-themed: what can go wrong if two different protocols use the same hash-to-curve function with an empty or shared DST?
options: The curve becomes singular for some messages
The same message can hash to the same point across protocols, enabling cross-protocol confusion/replay when message formats overlap
The mapping stops producing points on the curve
The output points become the point at infinity for all messages
questions.explanation: Without protocol-specific DST, different contexts can collide on the same curve points, making it easier to replay or confuse proofs/signatures across protocols.

questions.question: The Simplified SWU map in RFC 9380 (Section 6.6.2) requires A != 0 and B != 0. What is the practical consequence for curves like secp256k1 (A = 0)?
options: You can still use the same map directly; only Z changes
You must use a mapping that includes an isogeny step to an isogenous curve with A' != 0 and B' != 0, then map back
Hash-to-curve is impossible on secp256k1
You must replace hash_to_field with rejection sampling
questions.explanation: For AB == 0 curves, RFC 9380 uses SSWU on an isogenous curve E' with A',B' != 0 and then applies an isogeny map back to the target curve.

questions.question: What is the role of sqrt_ratio in the Simplified SWU mapping?
options: It computes the discrete log of a point
It returns either sqrt(u/v) when u/v is a square, or sqrt(Z * (u/v)) otherwise, avoiding retry loops
It compresses points by choosing a canonical x-coordinate
It hashes a message directly into a curve point without field arithmetic
questions.explanation: sqrt_ratio is designed to produce a usable square root without rejection sampling: if u/v is not a quadratic residue, multiplying by Z (a fixed non-residue) makes it one.
